cards.front: Since which Java SE version are record types available?
cards.back: Java SE 14
cards.extra: They arrived to make declaring an immutable data aggregate a one-liner instead of a hundred lines of IDE-generated boilerplate.

cards.front: What does the compiler generate from record Point(int x, int y) {}?
cards.back: Two private final fields, one accessor per component, a canonical constructor, and toString/equals/hashCode
cards.extra: That is the whole point: you declare only the state, and everything a correct immutable value type needs is derived.

cards.front: Which accessors does the compiler generate for record Point(int x, int y)?
cards.back: x() and y() - same name as the component, no get prefix
cards.extra: Unlike JavaBeans style getX(). You may override an accessor, most commonly to return a defensive copy of a mutable component such as a Date.

cards.front: What modifiers does a record's compiler-generated class carry?
cards.back: final, and implicitly java.lang.Record as its superclass
cards.extra: The final modifier is what makes a record genuinely immutable, so a record cannot be extended by another class.

cards.front: Can a record extend a class? Can it implement an interface?
cards.back: Cannot extend any class; can implement any number of interfaces
cards.extra: The reason for the first is that its superclass is fixed: the compiler makes it extend java.lang.Record, and Java allows only single inheritance.

cards.front: Why does re-generating equals() and hashCode() automatically reduce bugs?
cards.back: Adding or removing a component can never leave a stale equals/hashCode pair
cards.extra: Hand-written versions are the classic source of the bug where equals changes but hashCode does not, breaking use as a HashSet key, or the reverse.

cards.front: Which three things can you not add to a record?
cards.back: Instance fields, field initializers, and instance initializers
cards.extra: Each is forbidden because it would let instance state exist that is not a declared component, which would break the guarantee that equals/hashCode describe the whole state.

cards.front: Can a record have static fields with initializers?
cards.back: Yes - static fields and static initializers are allowed
cards.extra: The restriction targets instance state only. A record may also declare additional instance methods and static methods freely.

cards.front: What is a record's canonical constructor?
cards.back: The generated constructor taking every component as an argument and copying each into its field
cards.extra: It is the one the compiler writes for you. Override it when you need to validate state or defensively copy a mutable component.

cards.front: What is the compact constructor syntax in a record used for?
cards.back: Redefining the canonical constructor without repeating the parameter list
cards.extra: It has no parameter list, and the compiler assigns the parameters to fields automatically afterwards, so validation code is all you write.

cards.front: Can a record be serialized like an ordinary class?
cards.back: Yes, but serialization follows special rules that restore only the components
cards.extra: A record is serializable by implementing Serializable, and deserialization invokes the canonical constructor, so validation is honoured on the way back in.

cards.front: A record holds an instance field private final LocalDate born; not declared as a component. Does it compile?
cards.back: No - every field in a record must correspond to a component
cards.extra: Declare it as a component instead. The rule keeps the component list as the single source of truth for the object's state.

cards.text: A record is a class declared with the {{c1::record}} keyword rather than the {{c2::class}} keyword.
cards.extra: The components go in parentheses directly after the name, as in record Point(int x, int y) {}.

cards.front: A final class with final fields: what does it still need that a record gives free?
cards.back: Accessors, toString(), equals() and hashCode()
cards.extra: That is the boilerplate difference. A final class with a constructor is the sensible way to make an immutable class, but you still write the value-type machinery by hand.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: What two characteristics does every software object share?
cards.back: State and behavior
cards.extra: A bicycle has state such as current gear and speed, and behavior such as change gear or apply brakes. That real-world mapping is the conceptual starting point for OOP.
cards.example:
class Lamp {
    boolean on;                    // state
    void toggle() { on = !on; }    // behaviour
}

cards.front: In a software object, where does the state live and where is the behavior exposed?
cards.back: State lives in fields; behavior is exposed through methods
cards.extra: Methods operate on the object's internal state and are the primary mechanism of object-to-object communication.
cards.example:
class Bicycle {
    int speed;                  // state in a field
    void pedal() { speed++; }   // behaviour exposed as a method
}

cards.front: Hiding internal state and requiring all interaction to go through an object's methods: what is this principle called?
cards.back: Data encapsulation
cards.extra: It is what lets an object stay in control of how outsiders use it, such as a gear-changing method rejecting a value outside 1 to 6.
cards.example:
class Account {
    private double balance;                        // hidden state
    public double getBalance() { return balance; } // the only way in
}

cards.front: In OOP terms, what is a class?
cards.back: A blueprint from which individual objects are created
cards.extra: Objects built from the same class share matching components, just as bicycles of one make and model were built from the same set of blueprints.
cards.example:
class Dog { }   // the blueprint
// Dog rex = new Dog();   an object made from it

cards.front: One bicycle is what relationship to the class Bicycle?
cards.back: An instance of that class
cards.extra: A class describes the kind; an instance is the actual thing with its own field values. An application typically creates many instances of one class.
cards.example:
class Bicycle { }
class Demo { void run() { Bicycle mine = new Bicycle(); } }   // mine is an instance

cards.front: Why does the Bicycle class in a tutorial have no main() method?
cards.back: It is a blueprint, not a complete application
cards.extra: A class only needs main() when it is itself the entry point that the JVM launches.
cards.example:
class Bicycle {
    int cadence;                             // blueprint: state and behaviour only,
    void changeCadence(int c) { cadence = c; }   // no main() entry point
}

cards.front: Which of these is modularity, one of the stated benefits of bundling code into objects?
cards.back: An object's source can be written and maintained independently of other objects
cards.extra: Continue-and-pass-around is part of it: once created, the object is easily passed within the system.
cards.example:
class Parser {
    int parse(String s) { return s.length(); }   // written and maintained on its own
}
class Caller { Parser p = new Parser(); }        // uses it without knowing its internals

cards.front: A broken component can be swapped for an improved one without touching the rest of the system. Which object benefit does the tutorial call this?
cards.back: Pluggability and debugging ease
cards.extra: The analogy is mechanical: if a bolt breaks you replace the bolt, not the entire machine.
cards.example:
interface Encoder { }
class JsonEncoder implements Encoder { }   // swap the implementation, nothing else changes

cards.front: How does encapsulation relate to an object's internal implementation?
cards.back: Details stay hidden because callers interact only through methods
cards.extra: This is the information-hiding benefit. The implementation may change freely as long as the methods keep their contract.
cards.example:
class Counter {
    private int n;                 // internal detail: hidden
    void inc() { n++; }            // callers see behaviour, not the field
    int value() { return n; }
}

cards.front: In the Bicycle class, what role do fields cadence, speed and gear play?
cards.back: They represent the object's state
cards.extra: The methods changeCadence(), changeGear() and speedUp() define its interaction with the outside world, that is, its behavior.
cards.example:
class Bicycle {
    int cadence; int speed; int gear;   // the object's state
}

cards.front: What does code re-use mean as an object benefit?
cards.back: An existing object (possibly written by someone else) can be used directly in your program
cards.extra: It lets specialists implement, test and debug complex task-specific objects that you then trust and build on.
cards.example:
java.util.List names = new java.util.ArrayList<>();   // reuse an existing type
names.add("Ada");
System.out.println(names.size());                             // 1

cards.front: Can one real-world object contain other objects, and does that carry into software?
cards.back: Yes to both - a desktop radio has sub-parts, and a software object may reference others
cards.extra: This containment is why objects can model arbitrarily complex systems rather than just flat data.
cards.example:
class Engine { }
class Car { Engine engine = new Engine(); }   // a whole made of parts
